title: Which angles can bisection build, and is 65.5 degrees one?
description: A question from the book asks which other angles bisection can build and whether 65.5 degrees is one of them. Halving and adding give angles such as 135 and 67.5 degrees, and doubling shows that 65.5 degrees can never be reached.
teaching_notes: One idea: every angle made by halving and adding doubles into a whole multiple of 45 degrees, and 65.5 degrees does not. Watch for students who try to reach 65.5 degrees by repeated halving of a nearby angle.

video_script.why: The child can build ninety and forty five degrees and has not yet asked which other angles bisection reaches, or which it cannot reach.
video_script.substitution: The angles are built in the same way as the example in the book, by halving a right angle again and again, and by placing two built angles side by side.
video_script.anchor: What other angles can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct a 65.5 degree angle?
video_script.payoff_line: A sixty five and a half degree angle cannot be built by bisection

final_answer.value: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made; 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°
final_answer.spoken: angles such as ninety, forty five, twenty two and a half, one hundred and thirty five, and sixty seven and a half degrees can be made; sixty five and a half degrees cannot

never_show: the verdict on 65.5 before the answer line
maths_rules: Every angle built by halving and adding is a whole multiple of 180 / 2^k, so doubled k times it is a whole multiple of 180, hence of 45.
65.5 x 2 = 131; further doublings give 131 x 2^n. A multiple of 45 needs the factors 3 and 5; 131 is prime, so 131 x 2^n has neither.
Check: 22.5 doubled twice is 90 = 2 x 45 and 67.5 doubled is 135 = 3 x 45, but 131 lies between 90 and 135 and is not a multiple of 45.
video_script.design: One idea: halving and adding only reach angles that double into multiples of 45 degrees. The sixty degree and fifteen degree angles belong to a later topic and are not used here.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, halve the straight angle. One hundred and eighty halved is ninety.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Halve ninety, and we get forty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Halve forty five, and we get twenty two and a half degrees.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, place two built angles side by side. Ninety and forty five together make one hundred and thirty five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Forty five and twenty two and a half together make sixty seven and a half.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Many more angles can be built, and each one is made by halving and adding.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, double each built angle enough times. Twenty two and a half, doubled twice, is ninety.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Sixty seven and a half, doubled once, is one hundred and thirty five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is three forty fives. Every built angle ends up as a whole number of forty fives.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, double sixty five and a half. We get one hundred and thirty one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each later doubling only brings in more twos.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A multiple of forty five needs the factors three and five. One hundred and thirty one has neither, and twos do not help.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check the result. Two forty fives make ninety, and three make one hundred and thirty five.
